Here's a model that puts power where it belongs: with the people. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? Our electoral machine is strange, recent, corrupt, and deeply unappealing. Fortunately, human history gives us excellent alternatives. Here's a model that puts power where it belongs: with the people. | | | Jul 12 | | | | | | | | | | | | Twelve people. A courtroom. A stranger's freedom in their hands. We do this constantly, and we've done it so long we've stopped noticing how radical it is. We reach into ordinary life and pull out twelve ordinary people -- the nurse, the mechanic, the retired schoolteacher - and there should be a taco truck driver too -- and we hand them a power that would make most of us dizzy: the power to decide whether another human being walks out of that room free, or spends years of their life in a cage. We don't ask whether they campaigned for it. We don't check their resumes. We don't see who funded them, because nobody funded them. We simply trust them -- because underneath the whole solemn architecture of the jury is a very old and very radical belief about regular people: that given the facts, the time, and a real obligation to reason together, they will mostly find their way to something like justice. We stake a person's liberty on that belief every single day. And then we turn around and act as if those same people couldn't possibly be trusted to weigh in on the tax code. Let me say the awkward part out loud You'd be right to notice something. I am running for Congress. I am asking you to send me to Washington DC. And I am about to spend the next couple thousand words arguing that real power should be held more directly by you -- by ordinary people, together -- than by professionals like the one I'm trying to become. That's not a contradiction. It's the whole point. I am not asking you to send me to DC so I can "rule you." I'm asking because the system is captured, and the deepest repair I can imagine is to give it back. Given the choice, I would rather be a member of Congress who serves and empowers you than one who spends a career learning to hoard power - like the incumbent, and like most of them, frankly. If that costs me something with the people who prefer the second kind, so be it. This is the only kind of campaign I want to run. | | ---|---|--- The machine, built differently In my last essay, which went viral faster than anything I've written before, I described a political machine. The one that appoints its own governing majorities instead of electing them. That makes you clear a two-thirds supermajority of ordinary members just to overturn a handpicked committee of insiders. That decides who's "viable" by controlling the voter file and the software and the money. The one whose own lawyers stood up in federal court and argued that the Democratic Party promise to actually be democratic was mere "political rhetoric" -- not a real obligation anyone could enforce. The machine that returns House incumbents to their seats about 95% of the time (Senators close to 98%) and calls that "representation." (In a healthy government, that re-election rate would be 50-75%. An advantage...not a guarantee.) A lot of you wrote back with some version of the same question. Okay. So what do we build instead? Great question! Let's look at it. First:I 've spent twenty years doing things other than politics. Specifically, since the age of 15, I've invested my life in learning how economic, environmental, and sociopolitical systems work, how they interact, and how to design versions of them that produce maximum function & flourishing for the maximum number of people, on a thriving planet. Then, and only THEN, did I enter politics. Once it became abundantly clear that all of the economic cooperatives, affordable housing, climate resilience, permaculture and resilient agriculture, green infrastructure, clean energy, trauma-informed restorative justice, universal healthcare systems, healthy self-governance, and geopolitical sanity the world had to offer were never going to happen at scale without political change. So, reluctantly, I dove into the muck and maelstrom of US politics. Now to be fair, there are a LOT of passionate, creative, caring, capable, responsible, dedicated people involved in politics. I've been humbled and honored to be supported by many of them - volunteers make a grassroots campaign possible. But here's the thing - almost all of them have no real power beyond their own neighborhood. And the people who do have power? Almost all of them are structurally compromised by poisoned systems in order to acquire and preserve that power. Across the board. So, my systems-analysis mind kicked into overdrive. Recurring painful personal experience, directed at me as a public figure - a position I wasn't yet experienced with holding - taught me more than I'd known I didn't know. Pieces fell into place across the board. And one fact becomes absolutely unignorable... Our existing political machine selects for exactly this, every cycle. Donor capture. Incumbent lock-in. Political division. Gerontocracy. Lack of imagination. Party gatekeeping. An entire ecosystem of power and money designed to exploit people's hope, fear, and pain for power and private profit, without ever returning real improvements to your life. Put simply? This sucks. But I didn 't spend twenty years learning how to actually build a wholesome human civilization on a thriving planet, just to throw up my hands now. Hell no. So here. After all my study, travel, and depth of experience: let me give you this gift. Here, in this article, is a better way to design a political system. It's the best I've figured out so far. (Comment below with your thoughts and ideas!) This concept comes in two halves. One shapes who's in the room where it happens. The other shapes how the room actually works. You need both. First, I'll lay them out. Then I'll go into what it feels like to actually use this system. (Hint: it's wonderful.) Then, we'll look at similar endeavors that have been tried elsewhere in the world - and there are hundreds of examples. Then we'll take an honest, clear look at failure modes, and what needs to be implemented structurally to prevent them. And we'll close with a brief meditation on the wisdom of many societies and people who've come before us... and a pledge and a promise I carry as close as my own skin. Ready? Let's dive in. | | ---|---|--- Half one: who 's in the room There's an old word for the first half. It sounds technical, so let me introduce it, set it down and then mostly leave it alone: sortition. Selection by lot. It means you choose the people who deliberate not by election, but by a civic lottery -- exactly the way we already choose juries. The process is not "random" in the way that word is used to scare you. We don't just yank 535 names out of a hat. (Although, do you think we might actually have a more representative legislature, even if we only did that?) Sortition uses a "stratified lottery," which is a fancy phrase for a simple thing: you draw names in such a way that the room ends up looking like the country. Renters and homeowners. A welder, a nurse, a farmer, a schoolteacher, a lawyer, a landscaper, a kid three years out of high school sitting next to a grandmother three years into retirement. Rural and urban. Black, white, brown. Immigrant, native-born. Every income. Every background. Above all, the people who would never in a thousand years run for office -- the caregivers, the tradespeople, the night-shift workers, the working parents... the quietly competent people who hold this whole country together and have no interest whatsoever in becoming a brand. They become legislators, for a set period of time. And they are treated like the public servants they are. They're paid for their time. Childcare, transportation, interpretation, disability access, are all covered-- so that serving isn't a luxury only the comfortable can afford. They're given a domain, a policy question, some thorny topic that affects their lives and their communities. They're provided balanced briefings and access to experts who openly disagree with each other. They hear directly from the communities their decision will impact the most. And then they're given the one thing our politics almost never allows anyone: time. Time to learn, to question, to discuss, to seek out more evidence, to change their minds, and to eventually arrive at a decision they'll have to stand behind. That's it. That's the first half. It answers exactly one question -- who's in the room? -- and it answers it in a way that money and entrenched interests cannot get out in front of. Lobbyists and corporate interests cannot spend five years cultivating a legislator whose name won't exist until the day she's drawn. Half two: how the room actually works But a room full of well-chosen people can still become the worst meeting you've ever sat in. Anyone who's survived an HOA board, a PTA fight, or a city-council public-comment night knows that "gathering good people" and "governing well and making good decisions together" are not remotely the same thing. So the second half matters just as much -- and this is the part I know from lived experience, not just theory. It's called sociocracy. It's a way of coordinating group actions and making decisions together that I've worked inside professionally, running real teams and real budgets on complex projects reaching millions of dollars. This sounds like an exaggeration and simply is not: sociocracy is the most humane -- and honestly the most fun -- way of getting hard things done that I have ever been part of. The bones of it are these: People speak in rounds -- you go around the circle, every voice, one at a time -- so the loudest, most aggressive person in the room can't run the table, and the quietest person can't be steamrolled or just quietly forgotten. Decisions aren't made by crude majority, where 51 crush 49 and the 49 walk out resentful and already plotting the next fight. They're made by consent. And consent has a beautiful, practical definition. Not "everyone loves it." Not "everyone agrees it's perfect." Just: "good enough for now, and safe enough to try." And it directly answers what we've all experienced, and dread-- the one stubborn soul who blows up the whole evening by refusing to budge. "Consent" mode is precisely what disarms that person. Because an objection , in sociocracy, isn't a tantrum, and it isn't a veto you get to swing around the room. An objection is information : a reasoned explanation that "this will actually harm the work, or harm my ability to do the thing I'm responsible for." When someone raises a real objection, the circle's job isn't to out-vote them or wear them down -- it's to fold what they know and are bringing forward into a better proposal. A genuine objection makes the resulting decision stronger. A fake one -- "I just don't like it" -- has nowhere to land. Once the idea has been circulated around the room enough times that everyone is genuinely satisfied, or at least comfortable with moving forward, the circle effects consensus, the plan is adopted (usually with a set period of time for implementation before revisiting to see how it's working, which also helps alleviate pressure: there's a pre-planned exit ramp if the new plan turns out to not be going well); it's communicated to others, and implementation begins. Now look at what's not there: No voting. No hierarchy. No divisiveness; no factions; no knock-down-drag-out fight. No bullying veto. No external interests. No domination; no resentment. No incentive to lie. No incentive to smear or demean. Every reason to work together. Every voice valued. Every challenge or objection incorporated as the helpful and important information that it is. It's... transformative, frankly. Then comes the design that lets this model scale, and I think it's genuinely beautiful. Every circle has a domain -- a sphere of authority that is truly its own. And one rule governs the entire system: no circle takes an action that damages another circle 's sphere of authority. Not the small circles, not the big ones. Authority is nested -- circles within circles -- and coherence is never stamped down from a control center at the top, because there is no control center at the top. Coherence emerges , collaboratively, from the bottom, because each part is whole and each part is honored. How does this actually scale? It's surprisingly simple. From each circle, two people - the "double links" \- also participate in the circle at the next level of coordination. (Two people, to share the load, ensure honesty and clarity, and for redundancy in case of illness or incapacity.) A simple example: one circle is responsible for the domain of the Accounting department, with full authority and responsibility for decisions that affect that work. Another circle is responsible for Outreach. Another one, for Maintenance. No circle interferes in another's work, and two representatives from each of those circles also participate in the General Operations circle that provides overall coordination and support (formerly known as "management") across those departments. Because of the consent structure, in which objections are never overridden and proposals only move forward with everyone's consent, and because of the presence of the "double links," nothing the General Operations circle decides will ever damage the work of the Accounting, Outreach, and Maintenance circles. And from the General Operations circle, two people also participate in the Company Strategy circle, at the next level of organization above that. That could be the upper boundary of the system; there might be no direct circles interlinking with that one - or, perhaps... from the Company Strategy circle, one could imagine two participants at the City Council circle and maybe someone also serves on the support circle for the neighboring school; from the City Council, up to the County Council and the Bioregional Watershed circles, and... you get my drift. Why I keep calling it fun Let me savor this with you a moment, because this is the part nobody believes until they've felt it. I have sat in these rooms (and Zoom meetings). With and without sociocracy, and the difference is stark. People think sociocracy is fringe, but it's actually so much better than our standard ways of working together - which tend towards competition, hierarchy, suppression, and demotivation. I have run sociocratic processes with real money, real projects, and real stakes on the table. And what happens is initially slow, slightly surprising, then shockingly peaceful. The divisiveness drains out. The performance of toughness -- the chest-puffing, the point-scoring, the my-way-or-the-highway -- just stops being useful, so people stop doing it. The resentment that curdles a majority-rule meeting, where half the room leaves having lost? Gone, because nobody got steamrolled. The furious person who can hijack an entire evening? Their refusal only carries weight if it's reasoned and real -- and if it's real, it improves the outcome; and if it isn't, it dissolves. And that low, constant pressure to conform -- to not be the difficult one, to swallow your true objection just so the meeting can finally end -- that lifts too, because the whole method is built to want your objection, your point of view, your perspective and your lived experience, because it's important. Because you are important. What's left, when all that poison evaporates, is something I can only call joy. People laugh. They think out loud. They change their minds in public without shame -- one of the rarest and most beautiful things you will ever watch a human being do. You get real, practical progress, decisions that actually hold because everyone had a genuine hand in them, and you get there faster than the cynics swear is possible. Once you've learned a few basic moves and you're truly in it, it stops feeling like a technique at all. It feels like the most natural thing in the world -- like this is how we were always meant to decide things together, and somewhere along the way we simply forgot. | | ---|---|--- I 'm not selling you a utopia I've read too much history and sat in too many real rooms to trust anyone who does. So let me be honest about where this has actually been tried -- the wins and the losses both. Ireland has used citizens' assemblies for years, on questions from marriage to climate to the amendment that opened the door to its 2018 referendum. But in 2024, Irish voters turned around and rejected two constitutional amendments that grew out of an assembly process. A real defeat. And the arguments about why -- did interest groups steer the agenda? did the government garble what the assembly actually recommended? -- point straight at the same lesson from either direction: the chain from what ordinary people decide to what finally lands on the ballot has to be transparent and faithful, or the whole thing rots from the middle. We'll get into that in a moment. British Columbia , in 2004, did something no government had ever done: it handed a body of randomly chosen citizens the authority to recommend a wholesale change to a state's electoral system. 160 residents, drawn by lottery from every riding, met roughly every other weekend for a year -- a twelve-week learning phase, then over 50 public hearings and 1,603 written submissions, then deliberation. They voted 146 to 7 to recommend replacing first-past-the-post with a single transferable vote, and it went straight to the public in a referendum. And now hold onto something. That proposal carried a majority in 77 of British Columbia's 79 electoral districts. It won 57.7% of the province-wide vote. And it failed -- because the legislature had set the threshold at 60%. I want you to sit with that, because I have lived the small version of it. I told you in my last essay that I won 59.57% of an endorsement vote in a legislative district this year, and received nothing, because the threshold had been set at 60%. A province of five million people ran into the identical wall on the identical question -- whether ordinary people should get more power -- and lost by the identical margin. That is what a supermajority gate is for. It is the most elegant instrument ever devised for making a clear majority mean nothing, while letting everyone involved insist the process was perfectly fair. It works the same in a church basement in Auburn as it does across a Canadian province. And it is always, always aimed the same direction: at whoever is trying to move power outward. East Belgium built something sturdier than a one-off. The German-speaking community there -- about 78,000 people -- created a permanent deliberative body in 2019: a standing Citizens' Council of two dozen randomly selected residents, which sets the agenda and convenes citizens' assemblies on the issues it chooses. Members rotate off. Nobody accumulates. It never hardens into another permanent political class, because the architecture won't let it. It's the closest thing in the world to what I'm actually proposing -- and it has been running, quietly, for years, in a community smaller than Kent, Washington. That's the proof I keep coming back to. This isn't a thought experiment. It's a functioning institution. It's just not here. France convened 150 randomly selected citizens on climate -- a Convention drawn by lottery from a pool of 300,000 randomly generated phone numbers, sorted to mirror the country by age, gender, class, education, region. Truck drivers, farmers, nurses. They were paid the same daily rate as a juror. They met over seven sessions across nine months and produced 149 measures -- the crime of "ecocide," mandatory energy-efficient housing renovation, a ban on advertising for heavily polluting goods, a constitutional guarantee for biodiversity. And they did it while telling the experts no: a carbon tax was pressed on them at every turn by the specialists and by the President himself, and they rejected it -- one of them snapping at an expert, "don't treat us like children." So much for the theory that ordinary people can't help but be led. Macron had promised their proposals would go forward sans filtre -- "without filter." He committed to 146 of the 149. Then the lobbyists went to work in the ministries and the parliament, and the citizens' proposals were watered down and stripped out of the bill that was supposed to carry them. One assessment put the share that survived intact at around 10%. The people did their job magnificently. The machine ate the homework. That is the failure mode I most want us to design against, and I'll come back to it in a moment. None of this is fringe. The OECD has been cataloguing these processes for years; its database now holds 733 cases across 34 countries -- and from 1979 through 2023, at least 80,622 people have been chosen by lottery to sit in one of them. The permanent, institutionalized ones -- the ones written into the architecture rather than convened once and dissolved -- nearly doubled between 2020 and 2023, from 22 to 41, most of them at the local and regional level. The wave is already here. America is simply standing with its back to it. Now let me tell you exactly how this gets stolen I said I wouldn't sell you a utopia, so let me show you precisely how a system like this gets gutted -- because it has been, and the elites who did it were smiling the whole time. Whoever writes the question has already half-decided the answer. In 1999, Australia held a referendum on becoming a republic -- on cutting the last cord to the British Crown and having an Australian head of state instead of a monarch on the other side of the planet. And for most of that decade, a solid majority of Australians wanted exactly that. Measured support ran consistently above 70% - folks who lived there felt like the true number was 95%. Republicans outnumbered monarchists roughly two to one. This should have been the easiest thing in the world. It wasn't -- because of how the question was built. The model that went on that ballot came out of a Constitutional Convention where half the delegates were appointed by the government instead of elected -- convened by a Prime Minister who was himself a monarchist, and who then campaigned against his own referendum. Out of that room came exactly one option, put to the people as a take-it-or-leave-it: a republic whose president would be appointed by two-thirds of Parliament. But most Australian republicans didn't want a president handed to them by politicians. They wanted to elect their own head of state -- by better than two to one, in the polling of the day. So the opposition did something cynical and brilliant. It told direct-election republicans to vote "No" because they were republicans. Call it a "politicians' republic." Reject this one, hold out for a better one, we'll do it right next time. The strategy worked. The referendum failed, 54.87% to 45.13%, and the threshold needed to be 60%. It lost in every single state. Australia is still a monarchy today, twenty-seven years later, and no serious second attempt has ever come. A clear majority wanted the change. They were handed a question engineered so that their majority could not express itself. Now hold that up next to Brexit , which went wrong in precisely the opposite direction. There, the word on the ballot -- "Leave" -- was never defined at all. It meant leave the single market, or stay in it, or something else entirely, depending on which voter you asked. A vague question gathered up incompatible hopes into one number and called it a mandate. And the country then spent years in chaos, discovering that its people had voted for entirely different futures under the same word. Too specific, and you fracture the majority that agreed on the goal. Too vague, and you manufacture a mandate that nobody actually gave. Both are ways of extracting a verdict from the public while never giving the public a real choice. This is what I need you to see, because it's the pattern under every single failure in this essay: The danger has never been that ordinary people can 't govern. The danger is always that the people who already hold power keep control of the question, the witness list, and the follow-through. Look at them again. Australia -- half the delegates appointed, and a question engineered to split the majority. France -- 149 proposals from ordinary citizens, promised implementation without filter , then quietly dismembered by lobbyists in the ministries. British Columbia -- a supermajority gate set by the establishment just high enough that 57.7% of an entire province amounted to nothing. Ireland -- a chain of custody, from the assembly's recommendation to the words finally printed on the ballot, that nobody could vouch for. Not one of those was a failure of the citizens. Every single one was a failure of the powerful to keep their word. So if we build this, we build it with the locks on: Independent framing. The question cannot be written by the officials who convened the council. And the council must have standing power to amend or reject its own charge. If a hundred and fifty ordinary people study a problem for six months and conclude that they were asked the wrong question, they must be able to say so, on the record, and send it back. Their own witnesses. The council calls whoever it wants to hear from. A briefing binder assembled entirely by the people who commissioned the study isn't evidence. It's a framed curriculum. A duty to answer. Government must respond publicly, in writing, on a clock, to every recommendation -- and where it refuses one, it must say why, in its own name, signed, where you can read it. Real thresholds. Simple majorities decide. A supermajority gate is not a safeguard; it is a thumb on the scale, and it is always, always pressing down on the side of existing powers. I know exactly how that last one sounds, coming from me. I lost an endorsement this year with 59.57% of the vote against a 60% threshold. British Columbia lost an entire electoral system with 57.7% against that same number. Believe me when I tell you I have thought about that particular arithmetic more than most people ever will. None of these dangers go away by pretending they aren't real. So I won't. None of this is new Here's what surprised me most when I started pulling the thread. We talk about ordinary people governing themselves as if it were some untested startup idea. It is very nearly the oldest political technology our species has. The Athenians -- who handed us the word democracy -- didn't mostly elect their officials. They drew them by lot. They regarded election as the aristocratic method, the tool of the wealthy and the well-known, and the lottery as the democratic one, precisely because a lottery can 't be campaigned for or bought. Sortition isn't a break from democracy's roots. It is democracy's roots. In the Muslim tradition I've come home to, governing by consultation isn't a footnote -- it's a command. Wa amruhum sh ūrā baynahum -- "their affairs are decided by consultation among them." Wa sh āwirhum fī'l-amr -- "and consult them in the matter." And it was that civilization, across some fourteen centuries, that carried and enlarged the inheritance of Greece -- the mathematics, the medicine, the optics, the philosophy -- through Europe's long Dark Ages and handed it forward, giving direct birth to the Renaissance. Long before Europeans wrote a word of governance on this American continent, the indigenous Haudenosaunee -- the Six Nations -- lived under the Great Law of Peace: nested councils, decisions reached by consensus, leaders chosen and unseated by the clan mothers, and a principle we would be wise to carve over the door of every legislature on earth -- that you weigh each decision against its effect on the seventh generation yet to come. In the Horn of Africa, the Oromo people built the Gadaa system -- a democracy organized in generational classes, authority handed peacefully to a new set of leaders every eight years, with hard limits on how long anyone could hold power. Term limits and the graceful handoff I called for in my last essay -- worked out on the African plateau centuries before our Constitution was signed. And the consent method I described, deciding together without a vote that crushes the minority? The Quakers have practiced their own version for three hundred years, listening in their meetings for what they call the sense of the meeting - an emerging sense of agreement - rather than tallying winners and losers. Athens and Baghdad and the Haudenosaunee longhouse and the Gadaa assembly and the Quaker meeting house do not share a religion, a continent, or a century. What they share is an intuition our own moment has very nearly lost: that a people 's affairs belong to the people, and that ordinary human beings, gathered under the right conditions, can govern ourselves with wisdom. This is the basic concept of self-governance - the visionary experiment that started America. Set all of that beside the distorted and abusive thing we've been trained to call "democracy" -- pick a professional every few years off a menu two private clubs approved, then go home and watch -- and our version starts to look less like the natural order of the universe and more like the strange, recent, narrow, and highly unappealing exception it actually is. What I am actually proposing "Wouldn't it be nice" is not a policy, and you deserve better than a daydream. So let me be specific. I am not proposing we abolish Congress tomorrow and pull 535 names from a hat. Elections do real things we can't live without -- they let us choose a direction, compare ideologies and approaches, and, just as importantly, throw people out by name when they fail us. We should keep that. We need it. What I'm proposing is that we finally build the other half -- the half we've been missing: a real Citizens ' Council system, standing alongside the bodies we already elect. Start where people live -- at the county level. (Or even closer to home.) Build it out at the state level, in partnership with State legislatures. Then convene circles at the federal level. And there's no reason in principle it has to stop at a city line or a national border; the same nested logic could run from a neighborhood all the way up to problems that are frankly planetary - wherever the people want to take it. Councils of ordinary residents, drawn by civic lottery to mirror the actual public, seated for limited terms with real pay and real support so it's never just a rich person's hobby. No campaigns. No fundraising. No reelection to angle for. No donor to please. Organized the way I described -- nested circles, each with a genuine domain, deciding by consent, bound by that one unbreakable rule that no circle acts in a way that wrecks another's sphere of authority. Coherence that emerges naturally instead of compliance that's commanded and forced. And give these councils real teeth: the power to put a question on the public agenda, to force a recorded vote, to call their own witnesses, to send legislation back with a written finding when it reeks of capture -- and, in some matters, to decide outright. Built with the locks I described above -- independent framing, their own witnesses, a duty to answer, honest thresholds -- because a Citizens' Council without those is just a very expensive listening session, and I refuse to design one of those and pretend it's power. Then pair them, always, with the government we elect, the two halves checking and completing each other. Representativeness from the lottery. Accountability from the ballot. That -- not a slogan on a yard sign -- is what no corporate PACs, no foreign interests, no defense contractors looks like once you build it all the way down into the architecture. You cannot buy a legislator whose name doesn't exist until they're drawn, who can't run again, whose service simply ends. Capture needs a permanent, knowable class to sink its hooks into. This dissolves the handhold. The pledge I 've been carrying I have a tattoo in the middle of my back, over my heart, where I can't see it and mostly forget it's there. It's a pattern of overlapping circles -- the kind that nest inside one another and tessellate outward forever, the way they do in the geometry of the beehive, where a single unity radiates into endless coherent order, the same figure holding true at every scale. Inside it, I carry the Oak of Gernika -- the tree under which the Basques, the last surviving indigenous people of mainland Europe, swore generation after generation, to keep faith with their own liberties. It's the living sign that legitimate power is rooted in a place , and in a covenant , and in a living world that will outlast every one of us. For years, I described its meaning as "democracy in partnership with nature." That's true. But I understand it far better now than I did the day I chose it. I did not have the words, back then, for the vision I was marking into my skin. I have them now -- and they came from a governance handbook and a fourteen-hundred-year-old verse and a longhouse and a meeting for worship, all saying the same thing my soul has been drawn to the whole time: that power should be organized the way living things are organized. Nested. Reciprocal. Rooted in place. Self-correcting. Whole at every scale. With no single center it can't survive losing. I was carrying the architecture on my own body before I could name it. And I suspect you've been carrying some version of it too. Most people have. We were simply taught to stop expecting it from our government. But governments are living things too. So I 'm not going to ask you to adopt a plank I'm going to ask you to let a door swing open. We already trust twelve or twenty-four strangers with a person's freedom. We built a whole solemn architecture -- the jury -- on the faith that ordinary people, given the facts and the time and the duty to reason together, will mostly find their way to justice. Let's learn from our shared humanity, our shared memory, and the best of what human civilization has developed - so we can build something which will continue to serve freedom, justice, and peace long after we are gone. I'll leave you with one question. It's a question we have been very carefully trained not to ask: If we trust ordinary people with a human being 's liberty in a courtroom, why have we decided we can't trust them with the ordinary business of governing their own lives? Sit with it. That's all I'm asking today -- not that you sign onto a bill, but that you let yourself feel the door open before anyone asks you to walk through it. Because once you've really seen it -- once you understand that you were never meant to be merely the audience -- the way things are begins to look a great deal stranger than the way things could be. Care. Courage. The Constitution. ** You 're currently a free subscriber to "It's a Matter of Integrity" by Melissa Chaudhry. Republicans want to hand Trump a record-breaking $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget for next year ― more than half of which will go to for-profit weapons contractors. traveling across New Hampshire and meeting with Granite Staters in every
corner of the state.

Check out a few highlights from the trail ⤵️

We kicked off the Fourth of July by marching in parades in Amherst,
Merrimack, and Laconia. It was great to see so many folks out and about
celebrating our nation’s 250th anniversary and enjoying the holiday
together.

Trail to hear directly from community members about how we can strengthen
our trail systems and keep our communities connected.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260712_1.GTHGqg&refcode=em20260712-2&t=1005&akid=7695%2E582294%2EKUg2Gf ]Chris at South Manchester Rail Trail

organizers to open up our new field office in Laconia.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260712_1.GTHGqg&refcode=em20260712-2&t=1007&akid=7695%2E582294%2EKUg2Gf ]Chris at Laconia field office

### A tiny arachnid is spreading a devastating meat allergy and the clock is ticking.

| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e027aa5e-dbf8-401c-81c0-dfa4b894b962?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I have spent a career arguing that the most important signals rarely announce themselves. The skyscraper that tops out at the market peak. The pizza order that spikes in the Pentagon parking lot the night before a military operation. The private-label, single-serve trade-down in the frozen aisle that telegraphs a stressed consumer months before the macro data confirm it. Connecting seemingly irrelevant dots is not a parlor trick. It is, I'd argue, the only reliable way to see around corners and navigate uncertainty.
And the latest dot that has caught my eye is the size of a poppy seed that no one on Wall Street is watching: **a tick that is quietly building a short position in animal protein.** At the root of the development is a disease the tick spreads. It's a condition called [alpha-gal syndrome](https://substack.com/redirect/3e63572f-9de7-488f-9935-6f627389d192?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), or AGS, for short. It is an allergy (often severe, sometimes fatal) -- to a sugar present in almost every non-primate mammal. AGS essentially makes you allergic to meat.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/1f2d68a0-9249-42e8-8301-4533369a6306?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
You can catch AGS by being bitten. A tick injects alpha-gal into your bloodstream, your immune system learns to attack the molecule, and from that day forward a hamburger, a pork chop, a glass of whole milk, a gelatin capsule -- even certain medications -- can trigger hives, violent gastrointestinal distress, and, in the worst cases, anaphylaxis. A particularly cruel feature is the [delayed onset of symptoms](https://substack.com/redirect/a8d00fd9-db17-449f-ad6b-133e4d9b0ab2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Reactions usually arrive **two to ten hours** after the meal, long after the victim would ever think to blame dinner. A man eats a steak, wakes in the middle of the night throwing up and assumes it's food poisoning. In reality, however, his blood chemistry was quietly re-engineered.
This is not a fringe diagnosis, and recent data should catch everyone's attention. On July 2, the CDC published a [seroprevalence study](https://substack.com/redirect/54c86045-7cc7-4e8b-a890-c45df28397d0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that should alarm any consumer-staples analyst: **In the five states with the highest burden, an estimated** **24 percent of adults carry alpha-gal antibodies** , led by Arkansas at 31.2 percent and Missouri at 26 percent. Now, it is important to note that a positive antibody test is _not_ a confirmation of AGS. Only a [minority of sensitized people](https://substack.com/redirect/767e6779-0471-4d79-b60f-0e2c33742052?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) go on to develop the full syndrome, and the CDC's own authors warn against overdiagnosis. But for anyone on the lookout for potential economic fires, the magnitude of the kindling is stupefying. The CDC [estimates](https://substack.com/redirect/3e63572f-9de7-488f-9935-6f627389d192?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) as many as **450,000 Americans have confirmed AGS** , roughly 0.14 percent of the population. The sensitized pool sitting one bad tick season away is vastly larger.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/0952c739-ffa1-4eef-8ac9-5710d3cf53ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: CDC, as cited at [https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-to-know-about-alpha-gal-syndrome-a-red-meat-allergy-caused-by-tick-bites](https://substack.com/redirect/11a39e0e-7894-4dff-a3b0-4449cd7814c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Interestingly, there's also surging diagnoses in areas that have the ability to move markets. On Martha's Vineyard, the hospital went from nine alpha-gal tests and two positives in 2020 to [nearly 1,700 tests and 742 positives in 2025](https://substack.com/redirect/86bb9285-b5d5-4513-83d7-9a70dd21d48c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); that's a [positivity rate north of 40 percent](https://substack.com/redirect/4f3e8561-0e23-4a77-8842-0be65ada8541?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Nantucket sits on the [same curve](https://substack.com/redirect/06dd2159-fc47-451a-8258-7397c55a3dc0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). On Long Island, a single Southampton allergist now manages [more than 1,100 cases](https://substack.com/redirect/894b7be0-6dfc-4f11-9ee0-890e33b5ff51?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). These are not Appalachian hollows. They are the summer addresses of hedge fund managers, private-equity chairmen, and the people who set the clearing price of beachfront everything.
When a disease colonizes the Vineyard, Nantucket, and the Hamptons simultaneously, it has entered the bloodstream of American capital itself. And in November, the story crossed a threshold: a 47-year-old New Jersey pilot became the **[first documented U.S. death from food-induced alpha-gal](https://substack.com/redirect/b6f40b53-141c-468a-8ae6-950b35f333a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , collapsing four hours after a barbecue hamburger. One fatality is not a trend. But it is a headline, and headlines change behavior.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/a9378df4-e7f0-41b3-8f9a-b1b455dc4c74?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**So why now?** Follow the deer. The lone star tick's range is marching [northward on milder winters](https://substack.com/redirect/90805eb8-f897-49d3-ad99-9156f4719818?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and an exploding deer herd, and this spring the CDC reported [emergency-room visits for tick bites at their highest level since 2017](https://substack.com/redirect/6d308323-4ea7-4dd6-a91c-30750aa3af01?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But the lone star tick is no longer the only suspect. The CDC now acknowledges the [blacklegged (deer) tick can also transmit alpha-gal](https://substack.com/redirect/54c86045-7cc7-4e8b-a890-c45df28397d0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). This means the very species that blankets the Lyme-ridden Northeast and bites straight through winter may also be a problem. That quietly widens the high-risk area from the South to most of the eastern United States.
Regular readers know that I have a deep belief that every lens is biased, incomplete, and limited...and therefore insist on analyzing uncertain developments through multiple lenses. So what does a multi-lens analysis of AGS suggest?
**The market lens.** I run a frozen-pizza company, so let me confess my self-interest: pepperoni, sausage, and beef crumbles are mammalian. Every diagnosed case is a household quietly and (potentially permanently) exiting the red-meat market (and often the dairy market). This is not a fad diet subject to rapid changes in consumer sentiment. **It is involuntary demand destruction, one bite at a time.** The cattle, pork, and dairy complexes have spent years fretting over plant-based imitators and GLP-1 appetite suppression. They should add an arachnid to the watch list.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/2edc6f13-52a7-4b94-a64e-76af73d031b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Photo by [Erik Karits](https://substack.com/redirect/ac3ea7ce-fa8c-4ddf-964e-40e789d8f6cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on [Unsplash](https://substack.com/redirect/154d4654-84b3-4a80-a38d-50c57bb6ed77?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**The biotech lens.** Pfizer and Valneva just posted **[73 percent efficacy](https://substack.com/redirect/1e3cb7cb-58b9-4b13-884d-7f239fe41df6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** in their Phase 3 Lyme vaccine trial; Moderna is advancing [mRNA candidates](https://substack.com/redirect/f74855fa-570d-4254-8480-f7b53068c716?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to treat Lyme; and Tonix is testing a Lyme prophylactic. Notice the gap: every single one targets _Lyme_ , not alpha-gal.There is still **[no vaccine and no cure for AGS](https://substack.com/redirect/28f8caa1-d366-4b99-8445-ff0c80014306?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , only avoidance. But that white space is unlikely to remain vacant. As part of a new federal plan, the NIH is now [courting companies with products that could protect against AGS](https://substack.com/redirect/6d308323-4ea7-4dd6-a91c-30750aa3af01?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Layer in [emerging research tying alpha-gal sensitization to coronary-artery plaque](https://substack.com/redirect/0aa84c7f-f12c-4d8c-8aa4-e8a9ab5f337c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and the addressable population may dwarf the people currently breaking out in hives. And because the biotech and pharmaceutical industries tend to focus on large potential markets, we should all take notice.
**The social contagion lens.** As I mentioned above, this is generating headlines, and headlines change behavior. You don't go from nine tests to 1,700 in five years (as happened on Martha's Vineyard) unless people are starting to panic. Remember, a large portion of these are people proactively seeking an alpha-gal test because they heard about the problem. Regardless of the true positivity rate, concern about AGS is now a social contagion in the elite parts of the country with potentially large ramifications.
**The policy lens.** Increasing policymaker attention over the last month suggests greater visibility of AGS as a risk. Massachusetts [made AGS a reportable condition](https://substack.com/redirect/86bb9285-b5d5-4513-83d7-9a70dd21d48c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and Congress is [weighing legislation](https://substack.com/redirect/64444c98-992b-4086-a1d2-caacce2d9dff?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to classify alpha-gal as a major food allergen. Such a designation would increase labeling and foodservice training requirements. And in late June, HHS [unveiled a national plan](https://substack.com/redirect/6d308323-4ea7-4dd6-a91c-30750aa3af01?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to combat tick-borne disease. It funds a pilot program to eradicate ticks on animals before they bite, backs reauthorization of the Kay Hagan Tick Act, and sets a 2035 target to cut Lyme diagnoses by a quarter. Regulators and legislators are notoriously overburdened with requests for their time; the fact that ticks are getting attention should concern all of us.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/6fe01be1-eb03-4e8d-9f0b-a259f90f05c8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So what should an individual do? [Treat clothing with permethrin](https://substack.com/redirect/3e63572f-9de7-488f-9935-6f627389d192?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); use DEET on skin; tuck pants into socks in brushy terrain; run a full-body tick check within hours of being outside; cut back the lawn edges and leaf litter where ticks lie in wait. If you've been bitten and later feel ill after meat, get the blood test -- and if you're positive _and symptomatic_ , read every label, because alpha-gal hides in gelatin, broths, dairy, and even some drugs. Carry epinephrine if your physician advises it. Prevention costs a few dollars; the alternative can cost you, as one New Jersey family learned, far more than a hamburger.
AGS is an under the surface dynamic that justifies more attention as it may intensify into a more dramatic and disruptive phenomenon. While some might dismiss these developments as insignificant, my quick analysis suggests otherwise. After all, we can now link **a tick on a Vineyard deer, by an unbroken chain of cause and effect, to demand for animal protein, the biotech pipeline, and even an act of federal policy.** The dots are on the page. We need to connect them.
And perhaps most importantly, keep an eye out for little black dots on your legs.

A tiny arachnid is spreading a devastating meat allergy and the clock is ticking. | | | Jul 12 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- I have spent a career arguing that the most important signals rarely announce themselves. The skyscraper that tops out at the market peak. The pizza order that spikes in the Pentagon parking lot the night before a military operation. The private-label, single-serve trade-down in the frozen aisle that telegraphs a stressed consumer months before the macro data confirm it. Connecting seemingly irrelevant dots is not a parlor trick. It is, I'd argue, the only reliable way to see around corners and navigate uncertainty. And the latest dot that has caught my eye is the size of a poppy seed that no one on Wall Street is watching: a tick that is quietly building a short position in animal protein. At the root of the development is a disease the tick spreads. It's a condition called , or AGS, for short. It is an allergy (often severe, sometimes fatal) -- to a sugar present in almost every non-primate mammal. AGS essentially makes you allergic to meat. You can catch AGS by being bitten. A tick injects alpha-gal into your bloodstream, your immune system learns to attack the molecule, and from that day forward a hamburger, a pork chop, a glass of whole milk, a gelatin capsule -- even certain medications -- can trigger hives, violent gastrointestinal distress, and, in the worst cases, anaphylaxis. A particularly cruel feature is the . Reactions usually arrive two to ten hours after the meal, long after the victim would ever think to blame dinner. A man eats a steak, wakes in the middle of the night throwing up and assumes it's food poisoning. In reality, however, his blood chemistry was quietly re-engineered. This is not a fringe diagnosis, and recent data should catch everyone's attention. On July 2, the CDC published a that should alarm any consumer-staples analyst: In the five states with the highest burden, an estimated 24 percent of adults carry alpha-gal antibodies , led by Arkansas at 31.2 percent and Missouri at 26 percent. Now, it is important to note that a positive antibody test is not a confirmation of AGS. Only a go on to develop the full syndrome, and the CDC's own authors warn against overdiagnosis. But for anyone on the lookout for potential economic fires, the magnitude of the kindling is stupefying. The CDC as many as 450,000 Americans have confirmed AGS , roughly 0.14 percent of the population. The sensitized pool sitting one bad tick season away is vastly larger. | | ---|---|--- Source: CDC, as cited at Interestingly, there's also surging diagnoses in areas that have the ability to move markets. On Martha's Vineyard, the hospital went from nine alpha-gal tests and two positives in 2020 to ; that's a . Nantucket sits on the . On Long Island, a single Southampton allergist now manages . These are not Appalachian hollows. They are the summer addresses of hedge fund managers, private-equity chairmen, and the people who set the clearing price of beachfront everything. When a disease colonizes the Vineyard, Nantucket, and the Hamptons simultaneously, it has entered the bloodstream of American capital itself. And in November, the story crossed a threshold: a 47-year-old New Jersey pilot became the , collapsing four hours after a barbecue hamburger. One fatality is not a trend. But it is a headline, and headlines change behavior. So why now? Follow the deer. The lone star tick's range is marching and an exploding deer herd, and this spring the CDC reported . But the lone star tick is no longer the only suspect. The CDC now acknowledges the . This means the very species that blankets the Lyme-ridden Northeast and bites straight through winter may also be a problem. That quietly widens the high-risk area from the South to most of the eastern United States. Regular readers know that I have a deep belief that every lens is biased, incomplete, and limited...and therefore insist on analyzing uncertain developments through multiple lenses. So what does a multi-lens analysis of AGS suggest? The market lens. I run a frozen-pizza company, so let me confess my self-interest: pepperoni, sausage, and beef crumbles are mammalian. Every diagnosed case is a household quietly and (potentially permanently) exiting the red-meat market (and often the dairy market). This is not a fad diet subject to rapid changes in consumer sentiment. It is involuntary demand destruction, one bite at a time. The cattle, pork, and dairy complexes have spent years fretting over plant-based imitators and GLP-1 appetite suppression. They should add an arachnid to the watch list. | | ---|---|--- Photo by on The biotech lens. Pfizer and Valneva just posted in their Phase 3 Lyme vaccine trial; Moderna is advancing to treat Lyme; and Tonix is testing a Lyme prophylactic. Notice the gap: every single one targets Lyme , not alpha-gal.There is still , only avoidance. But that white space is unlikely to remain vacant. As part of a new federal plan, the NIH is now . Layer in , and the addressable population may dwarf the people currently breaking out in hives. And because the biotech and pharmaceutical industries tend to focus on large potential markets, we should all take notice. The social contagion lens. As I mentioned above, this is generating headlines, and headlines change behavior. You don't go from nine tests to 1,700 in five years (as happened on Martha's Vineyard) unless people are starting to panic. Remember, a large portion of these are people proactively seeking an alpha-gal test because they heard about the problem. Regardless of the true positivity rate, concern about AGS is now a social contagion in the elite parts of the country with potentially large ramifications. The policy lens. Increasing policymaker attention over the last month suggests greater visibility of AGS as a risk. Massachusetts and Congress is to classify alpha-gal as a major food allergen. Such a designation would increase labeling and foodservice training requirements. And in late June, HHS to combat tick-borne disease. It funds a pilot program to eradicate ticks on animals before they bite, backs reauthorization of the Kay Hagan Tick Act, and sets a 2035 target to cut Lyme diagnoses by a quarter. Regulators and legislators are notoriously overburdened with requests for their time; the fact that ticks are getting attention should concern all of us. So what should an individual do? ; use DEET on skin; tuck pants into socks in brushy terrain; run a full-body tick check within hours of being outside; cut back the lawn edges and leaf litter where ticks lie in wait. If you've been bitten and later feel ill after meat, get the blood test -- and if you're positive and symptomatic , read every label, because alpha-gal hides in gelatin, broths, dairy, and even some drugs. Carry epinephrine if your physician advises it. Prevention costs a few dollars; the alternative can cost you, as one New Jersey family learned, far more than a hamburger. AGS is an under the surface dynamic that justifies more attention as it may intensify into a more dramatic and disruptive phenomenon. While some might dismiss these developments as insignificant, my quick analysis suggests otherwise. After all, we can now link a tick on a Vineyard deer, by an unbroken chain of cause and effect, to demand for animal protein, the biotech pipeline, and even an act of federal policy. The dots are on the page. We need to connect them. And perhaps most importantly, keep an eye out for little black dots on your legs. | | ---|---|--- VIKRAM MANSHARAMANI is an entrepreneur, consultant, scholar, neighbor, husband, father, volunteer, and professional generalist who thinks in multiple-dimensions and looks beyond the short-term. Under the Trump administration's new rule, which they rolled out on Friday, destroying that habitat is now completely legal, so long as a corporation doesn't directly kill or injure an animal on camera while doing it. It is a masterclass in bureaucratic villainy, designed specifically to give the drilling, mining, and real estate lobbies a free pass to carve up our public assets without consequence. The situation is incredibly serious, but here is the good news: They are banking on you feeling too overwhelmed to fight back, and we have the exact game plan to prove them wrong. While environmental lawyers challenge this in court, Public Land Warriors is launching an immediate, targeted digital ad blitz in the home districts of the politicians who rubber-stamped this corporate giveaway. We are going to ensure that trading away America's wildlife heritage for corporate profit becomes a massive electoral liability. **" Immigration agent fatally shot a man in Houston during an enforcement operation, authorities say"** via [AP](https://substack.com/redirect/c61e2871-fdd1-4527-a66b-42e50b84962c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) - A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed a man in Houston after he attempted to evade arrest in his vehicle during an operation Tuesday, the agency said.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the man ignored commands to stop and attempted to ram an agent who fired his weapon in self-defense. The man's car struck an ICE vehicle, according to the department, which oversees ICE.

The statement identified the man as a Mexican national, **Lorenzo Salgado Araujo** , and said he was living in the country without legal permission. It said federal agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against Araujo and that he died at a hospital.

**" Job market, pandemic hurt Texas community college enrollment"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/3483e182-945b-4102-a8dc-00a3429933bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Sneha Dey** - Texas community colleges have struggled with enrollment over the past 15 years as many high school graduates opted to go straight into the workforce, but a new report points to signs of the campuses pivoting to stay relevant.

More students are graduating from Texas high schools, yet the state's junior college enrollment hasn't kept pace with that growth. Along with those choosing the workforce, students are increasingly going to colleges out of state, researchers with the Federal Reserve of Dallas found.

Texas community colleges have made small but steady gains in enrollment since the pandemic, signaling some success with recovery, their report found. Now the state has about 700,000 students enrolled in those schools, which is still down from about 750,000 students 15 years ago, according to state data.

In recent years, administrators have dramatically expanded dual credit offerings that allow teens to take courses at the community college that also count toward their high school diploma. They've also increasingly offered short-term credentials that can appeal to young people who want some training but are not in a position to get an associate's degree. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/3483e182-945b-4102-a8dc-00a3429933bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

This is the latest legal action taken in a growing battle over groundwater resources in East Texas.

**Kyle Bass** , a venture capitalist and owner of Redtown Ranch Holdings LLC and Pine Bliss LLC, is seeking to end a moratorium on large-scale water extraction projects imposed by the Neches & Trinity Valleys Groundwater Conservation District. The lawsuit, filed through Redtown Ranch and Pine Bliss, argues that the conservation district violated the constitutional rights of Bass and his companies by denying access to water beneath the land and also seeks an undisclosed amount of compensation.

Redtown Ranch and Pine Bliss, both funded by Bass' private equity firm Conservation Equity Management, filed permits with the Neches & Trinity Valleys Groundwater Conservation District to drill 43 water wells across two counties that, when fully operational, could extract billions of gallons of water from the Carrizo-Wilcox Aquifer. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/ce362ec6-2819-4898-882e-ae340c1b2083?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" James Talarico raises over $30 million in second quarter, campaign says, more than triple Ken Paxton's sum"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/987da7b1-4b0e-47c8-b432-dc3f43d9ac9d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Kayla Guo** - **James Talarico** , the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee, raised a staggering $30 million from April through June, his campaign announced Wednesday -- more than triple the amount brought in by his Republican opponent, Attorney General **Ken Paxton**.

The haul is a record total for a U.S. Senate candidate in the second quarter of an election year, Talarico's campaign said, noting he has now raised more than $70 million from over 1.5 million donations, including 780,000 individual contributors, since launching his bid in September.

"I'm honored to stand alongside more than 780,000 neighbors who are tired of being divided into teams -- red versus blue, left versus right, rural versus urban," Talarico, D-Austin, said in a statement. "We are uniting Texans onto one team to change this broken, corrupt political system and bring down costs for working families."

**" Talarico polling stronger with Texas' Black voters than expected, but enthusiasm questions remain"** via [KUT](https://substack.com/redirect/b06b1696-37d7-486a-a677-c76a75b93678?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Blaise Gainey** - It was standing room only at the Texas Democratic Convention when James Talarico, the party's nominee for U.S. Senate, was set to address the party's Black Caucus in Corpus Christi. But his introduction, given by Texas Coalition of Black Democrats chair Frederick Nickens, reflected some of the crowd's lingering hesitation around the 37-year-old candidate.

"We're going to be respectful," said Nickens. "Y'all might have some feelings about it, right?" Still, a warm round of applause filled the room as Talarico took the stage.

This scene at last month's convention reflected a narrative that has followed Talarico ever since he won the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate over Congresswoman **Jasmine Crockett** : that he could struggle to win votes from Black voters in Texas who overwhelmingly supported Crockett in the primaries.

But recent polling from The Texas Politics Project suggests Talarico may actually be in a stronger position with Black voters than public perception would suggest. The poll found 67% of Black voters surveyed said they support Talarico -- of note considering what those numbers looked like for previous Democratic candidates for U.S. Senate at similar points in their campaigns. In 2024, the group's polling around this time showed **Colin Allred** drawing 47% of the state's Black voters, while **Beto O 'Rourke** had 49% in 2018. _([KUT](https://substack.com/redirect/b06b1696-37d7-486a-a677-c76a75b93678?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Ken Paxton vowed to crack down on "illegal voting." He may have violated Texas election law."** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/cf824310-5add-46bc-b83d-d209a878b6d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Zach Despart** - Two weeks before this year's primary elections, Texas Attorney General**Ken Paxton** announced the creation of a tip line for the public to report people or groups suspected of voter fraud.

"Free and fair elections are a cornerstone of a thriving republic, and with the authority granted to my office by the Legislature, we will stop at nothing to uncover and stop any illegal voting activity," Paxton said in a February news release announcing the tip line.

The announcement linked to guidance from his office about election laws in Texas, which included a requirement to be a U.S. citizen, a prohibition on collecting mail ballots on behalf of others and a warning that "it is illegal to misrepresent your residence on election records or to establish a residence for the purpose of influencing the outcome of an election."

Despite his own warnings, Paxton appears to have used an address where he did not live while voting in six elections in the past two years, including in May's runoff that made him the Republican nominee for U.S. senator, according to records obtained by ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/cf824310-5add-46bc-b83d-d209a878b6d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Gina Hinojosa proposes sending every Texas household $1,500 in her bid to oust Greg Abbott"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/54551549-9a1b-4331-b3ce-c8d40502a653?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Kayla Guo** - State Rep. **Gina Hinojosa** , the Democratic nominee for governor, is promising to send each Texas household a $1,500 check drawn from the state's rainy day fund if she defeats Gov. "The government is broken," Hinojosa said Tuesday in front of Pyburn's Farm Fresh Foods in Houston's South Union neighborhood while announcing the proposal. "It is more, right now, a burden than a help for people. That changes when I'm governor."

The $1,500 one-time rebate program -- which Hinojosa dubbed a "corruption tax refund" -- would cost the state $17 billion, her campaign estimated. It would be drawn from Texas' rainy day fund -- which is formally known as the Economic Stabilization Fund and serves essentially as a state savings account -- which stood at a record $24.8 billion as of November 2025.

Her campaign pointed to estimates by the comptroller's office that the fund will grow by roughly $2.5 billion to $3 billion a year, and historical trends that kept the account at around $10 billion for several years before swelling after 2022. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/54551549-9a1b-4331-b3ce-c8d40502a653?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Interim Fort Bend County judge sues county attorney to keep top office"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/828fe0a1-6ab9-4821-9a8a-a052a3ef884a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Claire Goodman** - **Daniel Wong** , interim Fort Bend County Judge, filed a lawsuit Monday against County Attorney **Bridgette Smith-Lawson** , asking a district court to declare that he remains the county's lawful judge despite Smith-Lawson's conclusion that his appointment ended last month. The lawsuit asks the court to declare that Wong's appointment remains valid, that the Texas Constitution requires him to continue serving until a successor is qualified, and that Smith-Lawson exceeded her legal authority by directing county employees to treat his appointment as terminated. It also seeks temporary and permanent injunctions preventing further actions that interfere with his appointment.

Smith-Lawson said Monday she stands by her legal opinion that Wong's appointment ended when the civil removal lawsuit was dismissed and called the lawsuit "a professional bullying tactic disguised in a lawsuit." She said her office has a duty to advise county officials when it believes legal exposure exists and that a formal response to the lawsuit is forthcoming.

The dispute stems from Wong's appointment in April after visiting Judge **Jeth Jones** suspended former County Judge **KP George** during a civil removal proceeding initiated by a Fort Bend County resident. Jones appointed Wong to the seat. On June 16, George was sentenced to 180 days in the Fort Bend County Jail, five years of community supervision, and a $5,000 fine after his conviction for felony money laundering. George has appealed the conviction. After George's sentencing, the plaintiff voluntarily withdrew the civil removal lawsuit and it was dismissed.

Smith-Lawson subsequently issued a legal opinion concluding Wong's temporary appointment ended when the civil lawsuit was dismissed. In a June 24 memorandum to department heads, she wrote that Wong "no longer holds the legal authority to act as County Judge" and directed county officials to begin offboarding procedures, including revoking his building and computer access. **" Texas home insurers saw record profits last year as rate hikes slowed"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/2131ac7f-4238-4d41-822b-95a7a97ec13c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Megan Kimble** - Last year was a good one for Texas home insurers. That's according to the preliminary 2025 financial figures, which were recently made public. Insurers earned roughly 22 cents for every dollar in premiums they collected -- their best year in two decades. The record profit came after several years of double-digit rate increases for policy holders and flat or slightly negative returns for insurers, meaning they paid more in claims than they collected in premiums.

Statewide, rates increased by an average of 4.3% in 2025, according to the Texas Department of Insurance. That's significantly lower than the double-digit increases in recent years, though homeowners were still paying about 80% more for home insurance in 2025 than they were in 2020 -- roughly $3,500 for an average policy, up from $2,000.

TDI Commissioner **Amanda Crawford** said in an interview that she is "cautiously optimistic" that homeowners will see some relief on insurance premiums. Rates in Texas are among the highest in the country, largely because climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of storms. Given the profits reported last year, Crawford said insurance companies should "strongly consider whether or not a rate decrease might be in order."

"We're certainly seeing a leveling off," she said in an interview. "We haven't quite seen a decrease yet." There's little the state agency can do to force companies to charge less. Texas is a file-and-use state, which means insurers can change their rates without waiting for state approval. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/2131ac7f-4238-4d41-822b-95a7a97ec13c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_
